extracted.intended_audience: students, scientists, and educated readers interested in the philosophy and method of science
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for determining when conceptions and inferences count as scientifically valid; focuses on self-consistency, deducibility from normal perception, repeatability, and legitimate limits of inference (especially about consciousness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Science deals with conceptions (not only immediate impressions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Science is a classification and analysis of the contents of the mind; the scientific method consists in drawing just comparisons and inferences from stored sense-impresses and the conceptions based upon them. Not till the immediate sense-impression has reached the level of a conception or at least a perception does it become material for science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that scientific hypotheses often lie beyond immediate sensible impressions; scientists may legitimately reason about inferred entities (atoms, historical facts, other-consciousness) provided the conceptions are ultimately based on sense-impressions and treated critically. Anti-pattern: treating immediate sense-impressions as the sole field of legitimate scientific inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific validity of a conception
rubrics_metrics.description: In order that a conception may have scientific validity, it must be self-consistent, and deducible from the perceptions of the normal human being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-consistency illustrated by rejecting chimeras (e.g., centaur) once anatomy shows incompatibility. 'Deducible from perceptions of the normal human being' does not mean majority-derived — a properly trained normal observer placed in the right circumstances should be able to deduce it. Anti-patterns: accepting conceptions based on abnormal perceptive faculties (e.g., color-blind observer's conception) or on mere popularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeatability and corroboration by multiple observers
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations and experiments of science should be repeated as often and by as many observers as possible to ensure results have validity for all normal human beings and are not the product of abnormal perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where repetition is difficult or impossible, a heavier responsibility lies on the recorder and on the public to probe the evidence; one must question whether observers were trained, calm, unbiased, and in normal perceptive condition. Example: large-scale but contested experiments (Brown-Séquard) place onus on investigator to prove precautions and suitability of experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on recorder for non-repeatable or extraordinary events
rubrics_metrics.description: When an event cannot be repeated and is out of accord with customary experience, great onus is laid on the recorder to test whether their perceptive faculties and circumstances were normal and whether precautions were taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The public and scientific community must critically examine such reports, asking if observers were trained, calm, and unbiased. Over-doubt is socially preferable to over-credulity in such cases. Anti-pattern: uncritical acceptance of extraordinary one-off reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific validity of an inference
rubrics_metrics.description: The inference which is scientifically valid is that which could be drawn by every logically trained normal mind, if it were in possession of the conceptions upon which the inference has been based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stress distinction between 'could be drawn' and 'actually would be drawn' — historical scientific inferences (e.g., Darwinian natural selection) may take time to be accepted. Illogical minds may produce fallacious inferences rapidly. Expect logical training and shared conceptions for validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the 'argument from ignorance' fallacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The assumption that the strongest argument for a statement is the absence or impossibility of a demonstration of its falsehood is fallacious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided (manufacturing improbable justifications for miracles or pantheistic conclusions) illustrate that absence of disproof does not constitute proof. Anti-pattern: inferring wide conclusions simply because falsification hasn't yet been produced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doubt and criticism are safeguards of science
rubrics_metrics.description: Honest doubt and criticism (la critique est la vie de la science) are valuable safeguards of progress; prevalence of doubt should be seen as protective rather than decadent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns against any scientific hierarchy branding doubt heretical; promotes continual critique and skepticism as central to scientific health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits to inferring other-consciousness and will
rubrics_metrics.description: We may infer consciousness and will only where we observe machinery (brain/nervous system) approximately like our own and an interval between sense-impression and exertion; where no such machinery or interval exists, we have no right to infer consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inference of consciousness is reasonable in fellow humans and in lower life forms with similar nervous organization but is illogical when applied to matter without nervous systems or to beings in dissimilar surroundings (e.g., infinite consciousness outside physical surroundings). Anti-pattern: ejecting consciousness into matter or into postulated immaterial existences without any basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canon 1: Do not believe where reason cannot be applied
rubrics_metrics.description: Where it is impossible to apply man's reason (to criticize and investigate at all), it is not only unprofitable but antisocial to believe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Belief should be an adjunct to knowledge and a guide to action where probability, not knowledge, governs. Belief in spheres where reasoning cannot reach prejudices action in spheres where reason applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canon 2: Infer only from known to like unknowns in similar surroundings
rubrics_metrics.description: We may infer what we cannot verify by direct sense-impression only when the inference is from known things to unknown things of the like nature in similar surroundings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by rejecting inference of 'man in the moon' because physical surroundings differ; prevents overextension of analogy across dissimilar contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canon 3: Conditions for inferring tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: We may infer the truth of tradition when its contents are of like character and continuous with men's present experience, and when there is reasonable ground for supposing its source to lie in persons knowing the facts and reporting what they knew.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: accepting the tradition that Wellington and Blücher won Waterloo fulfils conditions; miracle stories or legendary claims often do not. Emphasizes source reliability and continuity with experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canon 4: Do not base permanent conduct on beliefs from inadequate testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: While in minor rapid decisions it is reasonable to infer on slight evidence, it is opposed to the true interests of society to take as a permanent standard of conduct a belief based on inadequate testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptance of beliefs as habitual guides based on insufficient evidence undermines individual responsibility for important decisions (example: assuming a cab will be on the stand when catching a vital train).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that conceptions be deducible by trained normal observers (clarification)
rubrics_metrics.description: A conception's scientific validity hinges on whether a normal human, trained in the proper methods of observation and placed in appropriate circumstances, would deduce it from perception rather than its negation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that scientific validity is not mere majority agreement; training and correct observational conditions matter. Use this to distinguish legitimately novel scientific conceptions from unfounded claims.
